summary: John Henry Wright was a scholar in archaeology and linguistics. He studied at Dartmouth and Leipzig under Georg Curtius, and held posts at Ohio State (1873–1876), Dartmouth (1878–1886), Johns Hopkins (1886), and Harvard as professor (circa 1887–1908).

John Herbert Harington was an Indologist and historian. He served as secretary (1790) and president (1825–1828) of The Asiatic Society, and as President of the Council of Fort William College (circa 1801–1823).

John Hick worked in philosophy and religious studies. His career included posts at Cornell, Princeton Theological Seminary, Cambridge, Birmingham, and Claremont Graduate University, where he was Danforth Professor (attested 1985–1989).
John Hope studied at the University of Edinburgh and later held a post there from circa 1761 to 1786.

Tibetologist and Buddhist studies scholar John Hurrell Crook studied at Southampton and Cambridge under Robert Hinde and William Homan Thorpe, and with Sheng Yen. He taught at the University of Bristol (circa 1963–1995) and founded the Western Chan Fellowship.

John Irwin worked in archaeology, Indology, and Buddhist studies. He served as Assistant Keeper (1945) and Keeper (1959–1978) at the Victoria and Albert Museum, and as a visiting professor at the University of Michigan in 1985.

John J. Holder, a scholar in philosophy and Buddhist studies, studied under Harry Krebs. He held a visiting research appointment at the University of Oxford and posts at St. Norbert College (attested 2006, 2018).

John J. Makransky works in Buddhist studies, Tibetology, and philosophy. He completed his PhD at the University of Wisconsin-Madison (1981–1990) under multiple teachers. His posts include Boston College (1992) and senior faculty advisor at Rangjung Yeshe Institute (attested 2007).

John James Jones was a scholar in Indology and Buddhist studies. After earning an M.A. at Aberystwyth University (1911–1914), he served as Assistant Keeper (1926) and Deputy-Keeper (1928) at the National Library of Wales.

John Jorgensen works in Buddhist studies, Sinology, and Japanology. He held posts at the Australian National University, Griffith University, and La Trobe University's China Studies Research Centre (attested 2019).

John Kieschnick is a scholar of Buddhist studies and Sinology. He held a post at the University of Bristol (circa 2005–2011) and became Robert H. N. Ho Family Foundation Professor at Stanford University circa 2011.

John Lane Bell is a philosopher who earned his D.Phil. at Oxford (1977–1980). He held posts at the London School of Economics (circa 1968–1989), Western Ontario (circa 1989), Singapore, and Cambridge (2001).

John Leyden was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Edinburgh, St Andrews, and under Henry Thomas Colebrooke. He was Professor of Hindustani at Fort William College (1806) and secretary at The Asiatic Society (circa 1807–1811).

John Lockwood Kipling was a scholar in Indology and archaeology. He taught at the Sir Jamsetjee Jeejebhoy School of Art (1865), and served as Principal of the National College of Arts and Curator of Lahore Museum (1875–1893).

John M. Koller is a scholar of philosophy, Indology, and religious studies. He studied at the East-West Center under Shri Krishna Saksena, Charles Alexander Moore, and George T. Artola, and was a philosophy professor at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute.

John M. Rosenfield was an art historian and scholar of Japanology and Buddhist studies. He earned his Ph.D. at Harvard under Benjamin Rowland, later serving as Harvard professor and Curator of Oriental Art (1965–1991).

John Marshall was an archaeologist and Indologist. He studied at Cambridge and under Arthur Evans at the British School at Athens. He served as Director General of the Archaeological Survey of India (1902–1931).

John McKenzie was an Indologist and philosopher who studied at Aberdeen, Free Church College, and Tübingen. He served as Professor (1908) and Principal (1921–1944) of Wilson College, Mumbai, and Vice-Chancellor of the University of Mumbai (1931–1933).
John McKerrell worked in linguistics and Indology. He served as a Telugu and Kannaḍa translator for the Madras Civil Service in 1804 and was an ex officio member of the College of Fort St. George.

John Morrison, who studied at the University of Calcutta, worked in religious studies and Indology. He served as Principal of Scottish Church College (1889–1904) and held lectureships at the universities of Glasgow (1904) and Edinburgh.
